title: Mors Lausi et Mezentii
titleEn: The Deaths of Lausus and Mezentius — Aeneid X.791–908
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Lausus, the young son of Mezentius, steps between his wounded father and Aeneas's sword, and his comrades cover the old man's retreat with a storm of spears. Aeneas waits under his shield like a traveller sheltering from hail, warns the boy off, and then, his anger rising, kills him. Seeing the dead boy's face, he is overcome with pity: he leaves Lausus his armour, gives him back to his people for burial, and lifts him from the ground himself. By the Tiber, Mezentius, washing his wound, hears the mourning and knows what has happened. He blames himself, the exiled tyrant whose crimes have stained his son's name, and resolves to die. He mounts his horse Rhaebus, speaks to it as a companion, and rides at Aeneas, circling him and hurling spear after spear into his shield, until Aeneas kills the horse and it falls on its rider. Mezentius asks only that his body be buried beside his son's, safe from his people's hatred, and takes the sword in his throat. So Book X ends. The poet's address to Lausus, the father's lament and the hero speaking to his horse have Homeric models, but Aeneas's pity for the boy he has just killed is something Homer's victors rarely show.
part: The Deaths of Lausus and Mezentius (X.791–908)

sentences.t:
Hic mortis durae casum tuaque optima facta,
siqua fidem tanto est operi latura vetustas,
non equidem nec te, iuvenis memorande, silebo.
sentences.i: Here I will not pass over in silence the fate of your cruel death and your splendid deeds, if the ages to come will believe so great an act, nor you yourself, young man, who deserve to be remembered.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, and the poet breaks into his own story to speak to Lausus, an apostrophe, as he did for Nisus and Euryalus (IX.446–449). 'Hic', 'here', at this point in the narrative. 'casum… facta', objects of 'silebo', 'I will keep silent about', used transitively. 'siqua… vetustas', 'if antiquity (the long ages) will bring any belief to so great a deed'; 'siqua' is Greenough's one-word spelling of 'si qua'. 'non equidem nec te', a double negative that stays negative: 'not (your deeds), nor you either'. 'memorande', vocative of the gerundive, 'you who must be remembered'. Elision 'tuaqu(e) optima'; prodelision 'tanto (e)st'.

sentences.t:
Ille pedem referens et inutilis inque ligatus
cedebat clipeoque inimicum hastile trahebat:
sentences.l:
He, his foot drawing back, both disabled and bound in,
was giving ground, and in his shield the enemy shaft was dragging:
sentences.i: Mezentius was giving ground, crippled and hampered, dragging the enemy's spear along in his shield:
sentences.n: 'Ille', Mezentius, wounded in the groin at the end of the last part (785–786). 'pedem referens', 'carrying back his foot', the regular phrase for retreating step by step. 'inutilis', 'useless', disabled for fighting. 'inque ligatus', 'and bound in', tmesis: the compound 'inligatus' split by '-que', a touch of archaic style; the spear still fixed in his shield hampers him. 'clipeo', 'in his shield', ablative of place. 'inimicum hastile', Aeneas's spear-shaft. The colon throws the weight onto what Lausus does next. Elisions 'clipeoqu(e) inimicum', 'inimic(um) hastile'.

sentences.t:
prorupit iuvenis seseque immiscuit armis
iamque adsurgentis dextra plagamque ferentis
Aeneae subiit mucronem ipsumque morando
sustinuit.
sentences.l:
burst forth the young man and mingled himself in the fighting,
and, of him already rising and bringing a blow with his right hand,
of Aeneas, he went in under the sword-point, and him by delaying
held off.
sentences.i: the young man burst forward and threw himself into the fighting, and just as Aeneas rose to bring his sword down in a blow, he came in under the point and held him off, checking him.
sentences.n: 'prorupit', 'burst forth'; the Latin Library has 'proripuit', 'snatched himself forward', the same act. 'iuvenis', Lausus, unnamed until 810. 'immiscuit armis', 'mingled himself with the arms', dative with a compound verb. 'adsurgentis… ferentis', genitive singular, agreeing with 'Aeneae' held over to the next line: Aeneas rising up to bring down a blow. 'subiit mucronem', 'went under the point', took the stroke on himself. 'ipsumque morando / sustinuit', 'and held (Aeneas) himself back by delaying him', with the gerund 'morando'; the verb is held over and stopped short. Elisions 'sesequ(e) immiscuit', 'iamqu(e) adsurgentis', 'mucron(em) ipsumque'.

sentences.t:
Socii magno clamore sequuntur,
dum genitor nati parma protectus abiret,
telaque coniciunt proturbantque eminus hostem
missilibus.
sentences.l:
His comrades with a great shout follow,
so that the father, by his son's shield protected, might get away,
and weapons they hurl, and drive back from afar the enemy
with missiles.
sentences.i: His comrades followed with a great shout, so that the father could withdraw under cover of his son's shield, and they showered weapons and drove the enemy back from a distance with their missiles.
sentences.n: 'Socii', Lausus's men. 'dum… abiret', 'until (and so that) the father might get away', 'dum' with the subjunctive of purpose, here in past time. 'genitor', the poetic word for father, and 'nati', 'of the son', set side by side: father and son run through the whole part. 'parma', the small round shield of a light-armed fighter, Lausus's. 'proturbant', 'drive back'; the Latin Library has 'perturbant', 'throw into confusion', a slightly different sense. 'eminus', 'from a distance', and 'missilibus', 'with things thrown', held over the line-end. Elision 'proturbantqu(e) eminus'.

sentences.t: Furit Aeneas tectusque tenet se.
sentences.l: Rages Aeneas, and covered holds himself.
sentences.i: Aeneas raged, but kept himself under cover.
sentences.n: Two short clauses at the end of a line. 'Furit', 'rages', put first: Aeneas is furious, but must stand his ground under the shower of spears. 'tectus… tenet se', 'covered, he holds himself (still)', behind his shield. The line ends on the monosyllable 'se', an unusual close that checks the rhythm as Aeneas himself is checked. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ac velut effusa siquando grandine nimbi
praecipitant, omnis campis diffugit arator
omnis et agricola et tuta latet arce viator,
aut amnis ripis aut alti fornice saxi,
sentences.l:
And as, whenever, with hail poured out, the storm-clouds
rush down, every ploughman from the fields scatters,
and every farmer, and in a safe stronghold hides the traveller,
either in a river's banks or of a high rock in the vault,
sentences.i: And just as, when storm-clouds burst and pour down hail, every ploughman and every farmer scatters from the fields, and the traveller hides in some safe shelter, under a river's overhanging bank or in the vault of a high rock,
sentences.n: A simile from Italian country life. 'velut… siquando', 'just as, whenever'. 'effusa… grandine', ablative absolute, 'the hail having been poured out'. 'nimbi', 'rain-clouds'; 'praecipitant', 'rush down', intransitive. 'omnis… arator / omnis et agricola', nominative singulars, 'every ploughman and every farmer', the repeated 'omnis' (anaphora) emptying the fields; 'diffugit' is perfect (the metre needs a long u), of what always happens. 'tuta… arce', 'in a safe citadel', here any secure refuge, explained by the next line: 'amnis ripis', under the overhanging banks of a river, or 'alti fornice saxi', 'in the arch of a high rock'. Elision 'agricol(a) et'; 'arce viator' does not elide, since v is a consonant.

sentences.t:
dum pluit in terris, ut possint sole reducto
exercere diem:
sentences.l:
while it rains on the earth, so that they may, the sun brought back,
work the day:
sentences.i: while the rain falls on the land, so that when the sun returns they may get on with the day's work:
sentences.n: 'dum pluit', 'while it rains', the impersonal verb. 'ut possint', a purpose clause, 'so that they may be able'. 'sole reducto', ablative absolute, 'the sun having been brought back'. 'exercere diem', 'to work the day', a bold phrase: to put the daylight to use in their labour. The detail makes the sheltering sensible and brief, not cowardly, and so it suits Aeneas, who waits under cover until the storm of spears is spent. No elisions.

sentences.t:
sic obrutus undique telis
Aeneas nubem belli, dum detonet omnis,
sustinet et Lausum increpitat Lausoque minatur:
sentences.l:
so, buried on every side by missiles,
Aeneas the cloud of war, until it thunders itself all out,
endures, and Lausus he scolds, and Lausus threatens:
sentences.i: so Aeneas, buried on every side under missiles, bore the cloud of war until it had thundered itself out, and shouted reproaches and threats at Lausus:
sentences.n: 'sic' takes up 'velut' from 803. 'obrutus', 'overwhelmed, buried'. 'nubem belli', 'the cloud of war', the shower of missiles, carrying on the storm image. 'dum detonet omnis', 'until it all thunders itself out', 'dum' with the subjunctive of expectation; 'omnis' is nominative, agreeing with the cloud as subject. 'Lausum… Lausoque', the name repeated in two cases (polyptoton), first accusative with 'increpitat', 'scolds', then dative with 'minatur', 'threatens'. Here at last the young man is named. Elision 'Laus(um) increpitat'.

sentences.t:
“Quo moriture ruis maioraque viribus audes?
Fallit te incautum pietas tua.
sentences.l:
“Where, boy about to die, do you rush, and things greater than your strength dare?
It deceives you, unguarded, your devotion.”
sentences.i: “Doomed boy, where are you rushing, attempting what is beyond your strength? Your devotion deceives you, and you are off your guard.”
sentences.n: The print has 'tua. ”Nec', the closing speech mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'tua.” Nec', corrected here: the speech ends with 'tua'. 'moriture', vocative of the future participle, 'you who are about to die', with 'ruis', 'rush'. 'maiora viribus', 'things greater than your strength', ablative of comparison. 'Fallit te incautum pietas tua', 'your pietas deceives you, off your guard': 'pietas' here is a son's devotion to his father, the very quality Aeneas is named for, and the line is often quoted. Aeneas speaks as a warning, half in pity. Elision 't(e) incautum'.

sentences.t:
”Nec minus ille
exsultat demens;
sentences.l:
None the less he
exults, out of his mind;
sentences.i: None the less he leapt to the attack in his frenzy;
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Aeneas's speech (see the note before). 'Nec minus', 'and no less', in spite of the warning. 'exsultat', 'leaps up, prances', a word used of horses and of eager fighters. 'demens', 'out of his mind', with the recklessness of youth; Virgil's judgment is pitying, not scornful. No elisions.

sentences.t:
saevae iamque altius irae
Dardanio surgunt ductori, extremaque Lauso
Parcae fila legunt:
sentences.l:
and fierce, now higher, the angers
for the Dardan leader rise, and the last for Lausus
the Parcae threads gather:
sentences.i: and now the anger of the Dardan leader rose higher and fiercer, and the Fates gathered in the last threads of Lausus's life:
sentences.n: 'saevae… irae', 'savage angers', plural, rising 'altius', 'higher', like a swelling sea. 'Dardanio… ductori', dative of reference, 'for the Dardanian leader', Aeneas, descended from Dardanus, founder of Troy's royal line. 'extrema… fila', 'the last threads'. The 'Parcae' are the three Fates, who spin, measure and cut each life's thread; 'legunt', 'gather up', winds in the end of the thread as the spinning finishes. Elisions 'iamqu(e) altius', 'ductor(i) extremaque'.

sentences.t:
validum namque exigit ensem
per medium Aeneas iuvenem totumque recondit.
sentences.l:
for his strong sword
Aeneas drives through the middle of the youth and hides it whole.
sentences.i: for Aeneas drove his strong sword clean through the young man's body and buried the whole blade.
sentences.n: 'namque', 'for', explaining the Fates' work by the blow. 'exigit', 'drives through', from 'ex-ago'. 'per medium… iuvenem', 'through the middle of the young man'. 'totumque recondit', 'and hides it whole', buries the entire blade. The word order sets 'Aeneas' inside the phrase 'per medium… iuvenem', the grown warrior and the boy locked together. Elisions 'namqu(e) exigit', 'medi(um) Aeneas'.

sentences.t:
Transiit et parmam mucro, levia arma minacis,
et tunicam, molli mater quam neverat auro,
implevitque sinum sanguis; tum vita per auras
concessit maesta ad manis corpusque reliquit.
sentences.l:
Passed through both the shield the point, light arms for one so threatening,
and the tunic, which with soft gold his mother had spun,
and filled the fold the blood; then life through the air
withdrew, sorrowing, to the shades, and the body left.
sentences.i: The point passed through the shield, too light a defence for such bold threats, and through the tunic his mother had woven with soft gold thread, and blood filled the folds at his breast; then his life, grieving, slipped away through the air to the shades and forsook the body.
sentences.n: 'Transiit et parmam… et tunicam', 'passed through both the shield and the tunic'. 'levia arma minacis', 'light arms for one so threatening', in apposition to 'parmam': a small shield for so bold a fighter. 'neverat', pluperfect of 'neo', 'had spun'; the mother's work makes the death a family's loss. 'sinum', the fold of the tunic over the breast. 'vita… concessit maesta ad manis', 'life withdrew, sorrowing, to the shades', 'manis' the '-is' accusative plural; the soul grieving as it goes recalls Homer's lines on the deaths of Patroclus and Hector (Iliad 16.856–857, 22.362–363). Elisions 'levi(a) arma', 'maest(a) ad'.

sentences.t:
At vero ut voltum vidit morientis et ora,
ora modis Anchisiades pallentia miris,
ingemuit miserans graviter dextramque tetendit,
et mentem patriae subiit pietatis imago.
sentences.l:
But truly, when the face he saw of the dying boy, and the features,
the features, Anchises' son, growing pale in wondrous ways,
he groaned, pitying, deeply, and his right hand stretched out,
and into his mind there entered the image of devotion to a father.
sentences.i: But when Anchises' son saw the dying boy's features, those features turning so strangely and wonderfully pale, he groaned deeply in pity and held out his hand, and there rose in his mind the image of his own devotion to his father.
sentences.n: Now the killer's pity. 'At vero', 'but truly', a strong turn. 'ora, / ora', the word repeated across the line-end (anadiplosis) as Aeneas looks again. 'Anchisiades', 'son of Anchises', a Greek patronymic, chosen for a passage about fathers and sons. 'modis… miris', 'in wondrous ways', a phrase from Lucretius (1.123, of ghosts 'pale in wondrous ways'). 'dextram tetendit', a gesture of pity. 'patriae pietatis imago', 'the image of devotion to a father': Lausus dying for his father calls up Aeneas's own love for Anchises (some take it also of his love for his son). Elision 'ver(o) ut'.

sentences.t:
“Quid tibi nunc, miserande puer, pro laudibus istis,
quid pius Aeneas tanta dabit indole dignum?
sentences.l:
“What to you now, boy to be pitied, for those glories,
what will dutiful Aeneas give, worthy of so great a nature?
sentences.i: “Pitiable boy, what can Aeneas the dutiful offer you now for glory like yours? What gift is worthy of so great a heart?
sentences.n: Aeneas speaks to the dying boy. 'Quid… quid', the question doubled. 'miserande', vocative of the gerundive, 'you who are to be pitied'. 'pro laudibus istis', 'for those glories of yours', 'istis' pointing to the person addressed. 'pius Aeneas': Aeneas names himself by his own epithet, as he did to Venus at I.378, and the word answers 'pietas' at 812 and 824. 'indole', 'inborn character, promise', ablative with 'dignum', 'worthy of'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Arma, quibus laetatus, habe tua, teque parentum
manibus et cineri, siqua est ea cura, remitto.
sentences.l:
The arms in which you rejoiced, keep as your own, and you to your forefathers'
shades and ashes, if that is any care, I send back.
sentences.i: The armour that was your delight, keep it; it is yours. And you yourself I return to the shades and the ashes of your fathers, if such things are any care to the dead.
sentences.n: Aeneas will not strip the body, though a dead enemy's armour was the victor's right in Homer and in Virgil; contrast Turnus, who takes Pallas's belt (X.495–500) and will die for it. 'quibus laetatus', with 'es' understood, 'in which you took delight', 'laetor' with the ablative. 'parentum / manibus et cineri', 'to the shades and ash of your forefathers', burial in the family tomb. 'siqua est ea cura', 'if that care is anything', to the dead. 'remitto', 'I send back'. Elision 'siqu(a) est'.

sentences.t:
Hoc tamen infelix miseram solabere mortem:
Aeneae magni dextra cadis.
sentences.l:
This, though, unhappy boy, will console your wretched death:
by great Aeneas's right hand you fall.”
sentences.i: Yet this, poor boy, will be a comfort in your pitiful death: the hand that brings you down is the hand of great Aeneas.”
sentences.n: The print has 'cadis. ”Increpat', the closing speech mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'cadis.” Increpat', corrected here: the speech ends with 'cadis'. 'Hoc', explained by the next line. 'infelix', 'unlucky one', nominative with the 'you' of 'solabere', where English would use a vocative. 'solabere', second-person future in '-re' for '-ris', 'you will console'; the death itself is what is consoled. 'Aeneae magni dextra cadis', 'by the right hand of great Aeneas you fall', ablative of means: to die by a famous hand was some honour in the heroic code; Camilla makes the same boast at XI.688–689. Aeneas offers it sadly, not in triumph. No elisions.

sentences.t:
”Increpat ultro
cunctantis socios et terra sublevat ipsum,
sanguine turpantem comptos de more capillos.
sentences.l:
He chides, unasked,
the hanging-back comrades, and from the ground lifts the boy himself,
with blood fouling his hair, combed as custom was.
sentences.i: Then, unprompted, he rebuked the boy's comrades for hanging back, and himself raised Lausus from the ground, his hair, combed and dressed as custom required, fouled with blood.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Aeneas's speech (see the note before). 'ultro', 'beyond what was asked', 'even': the enemy calls Lausus's men forward to take the body. 'cunctantis', '-is' accusative plural, 'hanging back' for fear of Aeneas. 'ipsum', 'him', the body. 'turpantem', 'disfiguring', with the dead boy as subject: his blood fouls his own hair. 'comptos de more', 'combed according to custom', the care of a young noble. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Interea genitor Tiberini ad fluminis undam
volnera siccabat lymphis corpusque levabat
arboris adclinis trunco.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the father, by the Tiber river's water,
his wounds was drying with clear water, and his body resting,
of a tree leaning on the trunk.
sentences.i: Meanwhile his father, beside the waters of the Tiber, was washing and staunching his wound, resting his body against the trunk of a tree.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, and a change of scene: Mezentius does not yet know. 'genitor', 'the father', with no name: the word carries the scene. 'Tiberini… fluminis', 'of the Tiber river', 'Tiberinus' the adjective. 'volnera siccabat lymphis', 'was drying his wounds with water', washing and stanching them; 'volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera', a poetic plural for one wound. 'lymphis', 'clear water'. 'levabat', 'was easing'. 'adclinis', 'leaning', with the dative 'trunco'. The imperfects paint a still scene. Elision 'Tiberin(i) ad'.

sentences.t:
Procul aerea ramis
dependet galea et prato gravia arma quiescunt.
sentences.l:
Some way off, bronze, from the branches
hangs the helmet, and on the meadow the heavy arms rest.
sentences.i: Some way off, his bronze helmet hung from the branches, and his heavy armour lay at rest on the grass.
sentences.n: 'Procul', 'at a distance'. 'aerea… galea', 'the bronze helmet', adjective and noun split across the line-end. 'ramis', ablative of place, 'from the branches'. 'prato', 'on the meadow', ablative of place without a preposition. 'quiescunt', 'are at rest': the armour rests while its owner cannot. The quiet detail delays the news. Elisions 'gale(a) et', 'gravi(a) arma'.

sentences.t:
Stant lecti circum iuvenes: ipse aeger anhelans
colla fovet, fusus propexam in pectore barbam;
sentences.l:
Stand chosen around him young men: he himself, sick, panting,
his neck eases, spread as to his combed-down beard upon his chest;
sentences.i: Chosen young men stood around him, while he himself, sick and short of breath, eased his neck, his long combed beard spread over his chest;
sentences.n: 'lecti… iuvenes', 'picked young men', his guard. 'aeger anhelans', 'sick, gasping', two words without a connective (asyndeton). 'colla fovet', 'warms, eases his neck', the plural 'colla' for one neck, as often in verse. 'fusus propexam in pectore barbam', 'spread, as to his combed-down beard, on his breast': the passive participle 'fusus' with an accusative of the part affected, a Greek construction Virgil likes. The old man's beard sets him against the boy. Elisions 'ips(e) aeger', 'propex(am) in'.

sentences.t:
multa super Lauso rogitat multumque remittit
qui revocent maestique ferant mandata parentis.
sentences.l:
Many things about Lausus he keeps asking, and often he sends
men who should call him back and bear the orders of his anxious father.
sentences.i: Again and again he asked after Lausus, and sent messengers time after time to call him back and bring him the orders of his anxious father.
sentences.n: 'multa super Lauso rogitat', 'he keeps asking many things about Lausus', 'super' with the ablative, 'concerning', and 'rogitat' the frequentative of 'rogo', 'ask repeatedly'. 'multumque remittit / qui revocent', 'and again and again sends (men) to call him back', 'multum' an adverb, 'much, often', with the antecedent of 'qui' left out; 'qui revocent' is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive. Some take 'multum' loosely for 'multos', 'many (messengers)'. 'maesti… parentis', 'of his sorrowing (anxious) father'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
At Lausum socii exanimem super arma ferebant
flentes, ingentem atque ingenti volnere victum.
sentences.l:
But Lausus his comrades, lifeless, upon his arms were carrying,
weeping, a huge man, and by a huge wound overcome.
sentences.i: But his comrades were bearing Lausus, lifeless, upon his shield, weeping as they came: a great figure, brought down by a great wound.
sentences.n: 'At', the turn back to Lausus. 'exanimem', 'lifeless'. 'super arma', 'on his armour', carried on his shield as on a bier, as Pallas is carried back on his (X.505–506). 'ingentem atque ingenti', the adjective repeated in two cases: Lausus is 'huge' in the heroic sense, greater than life, and his wound matches him. 'victum', 'conquered', the last word. Elisions 'soci(i) exanimem', 'ingent(em) atqu(e) ingenti'.

sentences.t: Agnovit longe gemitum praesaga mali mens:
sentences.l: Knew from afar the wailing, foreboding of evil, his mind:
sentences.i: His mind, already foreseeing disaster, knew the sound of mourning from far off:
sentences.n: 'Agnovit', put first: he understands before he sees. 'longe', 'from afar'. 'gemitum', 'the lamentation' of the men carrying the body. 'praesaga mali mens', 'his mind, foreboding of evil', 'praesagus' with the genitive; the subject comes last. The 'm' sounds of 'mali mens' close the line heavily. No elisions.

sentences.t:
canitiem multo deformat pulvere et ambas
ad caelum tendit palmas et corpore inhaeret.
sentences.l:
his white hair with much dust he disfigures, and both
to the sky he stretches his palms, and to the body clings.
sentences.i: he fouled his white hair with handfuls of dust, stretched both hands to the sky, and clung to the body.
sentences.n: The gestures of ancient mourning. 'canitiem', 'greyness', the abstract for the grey hair itself. 'deformat pulvere', 'disfigures with dust'; Achilles pours dust over his head at the news of Patroclus's death (Iliad 18.23–24), and Priam grovels in the dirt mourning Hector (Iliad 22.414). 'ambas… palmas', 'both palms', split across the line-end, raised in prayer or reproach. 'corpore inhaeret', 'clings to the body', 'corpore' ablative ('inhaereo' takes the dative or the ablative). Elisions 'pulver(e) et', 'corpor(e) inhaeret'.

sentences.t:
“Tantane me tenuit vivendi, nate, voluptas,
ut pro me hostili paterer succedere dextrae,
quem genui?
sentences.l:
“Did so great a hold on me, of living, son, the pleasure,
that in my place to the enemy's I let go under right hand
him whom I begot?
sentences.i: “Was I held by such a craving to live, my son, that I let the boy I fathered go in my place beneath the enemy's sword?
sentences.n: Mezentius's lament. 'Tantane… voluptas', 'so great a pleasure of living', 'vivendi' the genitive of the gerund; 'ut… paterer', a result clause, 'that I allowed'. 'pro me', 'in my place'. 'succedere', 'to go under', with the dative 'hostili… dextrae', 'the enemy's right hand'. 'quem genui', 'him whom I begot', with 'eum' understood as subject of 'succedere': the father names the son by his own act of fathering. 'nate', vocative, 'son'. Elision 'm(e) hostili'.

sentences.t:
Tuane haec genitor per volnera servor,
morte tua vivens?
sentences.l:
Through these your wounds, I, the father, am I saved,
by your death living?
sentences.i: Am I, your father, saved by these wounds of yours, alive because you are dead?
sentences.n: 'Tuane haec… per volnera', 'through these wounds of yours', with '-ne' putting the question on the emphatic 'tua'. 'genitor', in apposition to the subject of 'servor', 'I, the father, am saved'. 'morte tua vivens', 'living by your death', the antithesis of life and death closing the question. The father saved by the son reverses the order of nature: a parent should die first. Elision 'Tuan(e) haec'.

sentences.t:
Heu, nunc misero mihi demum
exitium infelix, nunc alte volnus adactum!
sentences.l:
Alas, now to me, wretched, at last
ruin is unhappy, now deep the wound driven in!
sentences.i: Alas, only now has ruin truly come upon me in my misery, only now is the wound driven deep!
sentences.n: 'nunc… demum', 'now at last'. 'misero mihi', dative of reference. 'exitium infelix', 'ruin (is) unhappy', with 'est' understood: his own wound was nothing; this is the real destruction. Some editors read 'exilium', 'exile', meaning that only now is his banishment bitter, which suits 852; Greenough prints 'exitium', and the Latin Library agrees. 'alte… adactum', 'driven in deep', with 'est' understood. The repeated 'nunc' marks the sudden realisation. Elision 'exiti(um) infelix'.

sentences.t:
Idem ego, nate, tuum maculavi crimine nomen,
pulsus ob invidiam solio sceptrisque paternis.
sentences.l:
I too, son, your name have stained with my crime,
driven out through hatred from the throne and sceptre of my fathers.
sentences.i: It was I, too, my son, who stained your name with my guilt, driven by my people's hatred from the throne and the sceptre of my fathers.
sentences.n: 'Idem ego', 'I the same', 'I also': the father who caused his death has also shamed his name. 'maculavi crimine', 'stained with (my) crime'. 'pulsus ob invidiam', 'driven out because of hatred': the people of Caere rose against his cruelty (VIII.481–495). 'solio sceptrisque paternis', ablatives of separation, 'from the throne and the ancestral sceptre', 'sceptris' a poetic plural. Elision 'Id(em) ego'.

sentences.t: Debueram patriae poenas odiisque meorum:
sentences.l: I had owed to my country punishment, and to the hatreds of my own:
sentences.i: I owed my country a penalty, and my people's hatred its due:
sentences.n: 'Debueram', pluperfect, 'I had owed', in the sense 'I ought long since to have paid'. 'poenas… patriae… odiisque meorum', 'penalties to my country and to the hatreds of my own people', 'meorum' masculine, 'of my own', his former subjects. Mezentius, the scorner of the gods, now owns his guilt; Virgil gives him a late dignity. No elisions.

sentences.t: omnis per mortis animam sontem ipse dedissem!
sentences.l: through every death my guilty life I myself should have given!
sentences.i: I should have given up this guilty life myself, through every kind of death!
sentences.n: 'omnis per mortis', 'through all deaths', 'omnis… mortis' accusative plurals in '-is' (you have seen this often), with 'per' set between them. 'animam sontem', 'my guilty soul'. 'ipse', 'I myself', not my son. 'dedissem', pluperfect subjunctive of an obligation not met in past time, 'I should have given'. His people had demanded him for execution (VIII.494–495). Elision 'sont(em) ipse'.

sentences.t: Nunc vivo neque adhuc homines lucemque relinquo.
sentences.l: Now I live, and not yet men and the light do I leave.
sentences.i: And here I am, alive, not yet gone from mankind and the daylight.
sentences.n: 'Nunc', 'as it is'. 'neque adhuc', 'and not yet'. 'homines lucemque', 'men and the light', the world of the living; to see the light is to be alive, in Homer and in Virgil. The line is plain and slow, with no ornament. Elision 'nequ(e) adhuc'.

sentences.t: Sed linquam.
sentences.l: But I will leave them.”
sentences.i: But go I will.”
sentences.n: The print has 'linquam. ”Simul', the closing speech mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'linquam.” Simul', corrected here: the speech ends with 'linquam'. 'Sed linquam', 'but I will leave', the simple verb 'linquo' picking up the compound 'relinquo' of the line before; Virgil often repeats a compound with its simple verb. Two words, a short, decided sentence: he resolves to die. No elisions.

sentences.t:
”Simul hoc dicens attollit in aegrum
se femur et, quamvis dolor alto volnere tardet,
haud deiectus equum duci iubet.
sentences.l:
At once, saying this, he raises onto his sick
thigh himself, and, though the pain from the deep wound slows him,
not cast down, his horse to be led he orders.
sentences.i: As he spoke he raised himself on his wounded thigh and, though the pain of the deep wound held him back, undaunted he ordered his horse to be brought.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Mezentius's speech (see the note before). 'Simul… dicens', 'at the same time saying'. 'attollit… se', 'lifts himself', with 'in aegrum… femur', 'onto his sick thigh', wounded near the groin. 'quamvis… tardet', subjunctive with 'quamvis', 'although'; the Latin Library reads 'quamquam vis… tardat', 'although his strength is slowed', a slightly different sense. 'haud deiectus', 'not cast down', in body or spirit. 'equum duci', accusative and infinitive with 'iubet'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Hoc decus illi,
hoc solamen erat; bellis hoc victor abibat
omnibus.
sentences.l:
This was the pride to him,
this the comfort; on this from wars as victor he used to come away,
all of them.
sentences.i: This horse was his glory, this his comfort; on its back he had come home the victor from every war.
sentences.n: 'Hoc… hoc… hoc', the horse named three times by the pronoun alone (anaphora). 'decus illi', 'a glory to him', dative of possession. 'solamen', 'comfort'. 'bellis… abibat / omnibus', 'he used to come away (victor) from all wars', the imperfect of habit, with 'omnibus' held over to the next line to complete the boast. 'hoc', ablative, 'on this', the horse. No elisions.

sentences.t: Adloquitur maerentem et talibus infit:
sentences.l: He addresses the grieving one, and with such words begins:
sentences.i: He spoke to the grieving horse and began with these words:
sentences.n: 'maerentem', 'grieving', the horse: Achilles' immortal horses weep for Patroclus (Iliad 17.426–440), and Achilles speaks to his horses before battle (Iliad 19.400–403), as Hector does to his (Iliad 8.185–197). 'talibus infit', 'begins with such (words)': 'infit' is an old defective verb found almost only in this form, 'he begins (to speak)'. Elision 'maerent(em) et'.

sentences.t:
“Rhaebe, diu, res siqua diu mortalibus ulla est,
viximus.
sentences.l:
“Rhaebus, long — if anything is long for mortals at all —
have we lived.
sentences.i: “Rhaebus, our life has been a long one, if any mortal thing can be said to last long.
sentences.n: 'Rhaebe', vocative of the horse's name. 'diu… diu', the word repeated: the clause 'res siqua diu mortalibus ulla est', 'if any thing at all is lasting for mortals', cuts in before the verb. 'viximus', 'we have lived', held over to the next line, and plural: horse and rider as companions. The perfect can also carry the sense 'our life is done'. Prodelision 'ulla (e)st'.

sentences.t:
Aut hodie victor spolia illa cruenti
et caput Aeneae referes Lausique dolorum
ultor eris mecum aut, aperit si nulla viam vis,
occumbes pariter;
sentences.l:
Either today, victor, those spoils of the bloody man
and the head of Aeneas you will bring back, and of Lausus's sufferings
the avenger you will be with me, or, if opens no way any force,
you will fall alongside;
sentences.i: Either today you will carry back in triumph the spoils and the head of bloodstained Aeneas, and avenge Lausus's sufferings with me, or, if no force can open a way, you will fall at my side;
sentences.n: 'Aut… aut', the two outcomes. 'victor', in apposition to the subject, 'as victor'. 'spolia illa', 'those (famous) spoils', Aeneas's armour. 'cruenti… Aeneae', 'of bloody Aeneas', stained with Lausus's blood. 'caput… referes', carrying back an enemy's head, a savage trophy. 'Lausique dolorum / ultor', 'avenger of Lausus's pains'. 'aperit si nulla viam vis', 'if no force opens the way', with 'si' set late in its clause. 'occumbes', 'you will fall (in death)'; 'pariter', 'equally, together'. Elisions 'spoli(a) illa', 'mec(um) aut'.

sentences.t:
neque enim, fortissime, credo,
iussa aliena pati et dominos dignabere Teucros.”
sentences.l:
for not, bravest one, I believe,
commands of another to suffer and masters will you deign, the Teucrians.”
sentences.i: for I do not believe, brave heart, that you will consent to bear a stranger's orders and take Trojans for your masters.”
sentences.n: 'neque enim', 'for not'. 'fortissime', vocative, 'bravest one', said to a horse. 'credo', parenthetic, 'I believe'. 'dignabere', second-person future in '-re', 'you will deign', with two objects: the infinitive 'pati', 'to suffer', and the accusative 'dominos… Teucros', 'Teucrians as masters'. 'iussa aliena', 'another's commands'. The horse is given its master's pride. Elisions 'nequ(e) enim', 'iuss(a) aliena', 'pat(i) et'.

sentences.t:
Dixit et exceptus tergo consueta locavit
membra manusque ambas iaculis oneravit acutis,
aere caput fulgens cristaque hirsutus equina.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and, taken up on its back, his accustomed he settled
limbs, and his hands, both, with javelins he loaded, sharp,
with bronze, as to his head, gleaming, and with a crest shaggy, of horsehair.
sentences.i: He spoke, and the horse took him on its back; he settled his limbs in the familiar seat and loaded both hands with sharp javelins, his head shining with bronze, bristling with a crest of horsehair.
sentences.n: 'exceptus tergo', 'taken up on its back', 'tergo' ablative of place. 'consueta… membra', 'his accustomed limbs', in the seat they knew. 'iaculis… acutis', 'sharp javelins', enclosing the verb. 'aere caput fulgens', 'gleaming as to his head with bronze': 'caput' is an accusative of respect, a Greek construction (you saw 'fusus… barbam' at 838); he has taken his helmet down from the tree. 'cristaque hirsutus equina', 'shaggy with a horsehair crest'. Elisions 'manusqu(e) ambas', 'cristaqu(e) hirsutus'.

sentences.t: Sic cursum in medios rapidus dedit:
sentences.l: So his course into the midst swiftly he gave:
sentences.i: So armed, he charged at speed into the thick of the enemy:
sentences.n: 'Sic', 'so (armed)', 'thus'. 'cursum… dedit', 'gave his course', galloped. 'in medios', 'into the midst', with 'hostes' understood. 'rapidus', an adjective doing the work of an adverb, 'swiftly'. The colon opens onto his state of mind in the lines that follow. Elision 'curs(um) in'.

sentences.t:
aestuat ingens
uno in corde pudor mixtoque insania luctu,
[et furiis agitatus amor et conscia virtus.]
sentences.l:
there surges, vast,
in one heart shame, and madness with grief mixed,
[and love by furies driven, and valour conscious of itself.]
sentences.i: in that one heart there surged a vast shame, and madness mingled with grief, [and love goaded by the Furies, and valour that knew its own worth.]
sentences.n: 'aestuat', 'surges, boils', like the sea; 'ingens… pudor', 'vast shame', at having let his son die for him. 'uno in corde', 'in one heart', all these at once. 'mixtoque insania luctu', 'and madness, with grief mixed in', ablative absolute. Line 872 is bracketed by Greenough as spurious, and the Latin Library omits it: the same three lines, with 872, describe Turnus at XII.666–668, and the line was probably copied here from there. 'conscia virtus', 'valour conscious (of itself)'. Elisions 'un(o) in', 'mixtoqu(e) insania'.

sentences.t: Atque hic Aenean magna ter voce vocavit.
sentences.l: And here Aeneas with a great voice three times he called.
sentences.i: And there he called on Aeneas three times in a loud voice.
sentences.n: 'Aenean', the Greek accusative of 'Aeneas'. 'ter', 'three times', a number of ritual and of challenge. 'magna… voce vocavit', 'called with a great voice', a noun and verb from the same root side by side, an old Latin flourish (figura etymologica). This is a challenge to single combat. Elision 'Atqu(e) hic'.

sentences.t: Aeneas agnovit enim laetusque precatur:
sentences.l: Aeneas knew him indeed, and gladly prays:
sentences.i: Aeneas knew that voice, and prayed with joy:
sentences.n: 'agnovit', 'recognised', the voice and the challenge. 'enim', here in its old sense, 'indeed, truly', not 'for'; Virgil keeps this early Latin use now and then. 'laetus', 'glad', at last the chance to meet him. 'precatur', 'prays', the prayer that follows. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Sic pater ille deum faciat, sic altus Apollo,
incipias conferre manum.”
sentences.l:
“So may that father of the gods bring it about, so high Apollo:
may you begin to join hand.”
sentences.i: “So may the great father of the gods grant it, so may Apollo on high: come, begin, and meet me hand to hand.”
sentences.n: 'Sic… faciat', 'so may he make it', the wish-subjunctive, a formula of prayer. 'pater ille deum', 'that (great) father of the gods', Jupiter, 'deum' the old genitive plural (you have seen this often). 'altus Apollo', 'lofty Apollo', a patron of Troy. 'incipias', a jussive subjunctive, 'may you begin'. 'conferre manum', 'to join hand (with mine)', to fight at close quarters. Line 876 is one of the half-lines Virgil left unfinished. No elisions.

sentences.t: Tantum effatus et infesta subit obvius hasta.
sentences.l: So much having spoken, he goes up to meet him with hostile spear.
sentences.i: No more than that he said, and went to meet him with levelled spear.
sentences.n: 'Tantum effatus', 'having spoken only so much', from 'effor', a solemn verb of speaking. 'infesta… hasta', 'with hostile spear', levelled for attack, ablative of manner, framing the second half of the line. 'subit obvius', 'comes up to meet (him)', 'obvius' an adjective with the force of an adverb. Elision 'Tant(um) effatus'.

sentences.t:
Ille autem: “Quid me erepto, saevissime, nato
terres?
sentences.l:
He, however: “Why me, with snatched away, most savage one, my son,
do you terrify?
sentences.i: But Mezentius answered: “Why do you try to frighten me, cruellest of men, now that you have robbed me of my son?
sentences.n: 'Ille autem', with the verb of speaking left out (you have seen this often). 'erepto… nato', ablative absolute, 'my son having been snatched away', with 'me' the object of 'terres'. 'saevissime', vocative, 'most cruel': the cruel tyrant now calls Aeneas cruel. 'terres', 'do you frighten', held over to the next line. Elisions 'Ill(e) autem', 'm(e) erepto'.

sentences.t: Haec via sola fuit, qua perdere posses.
sentences.l: This the only way was, by which to destroy me you could.
sentences.i: There was one road only to my ruin, and you have taken it.
sentences.n: 'Haec via sola fuit', 'this was the only road': the killing of his son. 'qua perdere posses', 'by which you could destroy (me)', a relative clause with the subjunctive, 'perdere' with its object understood. Mezentius means that death holds no fear for him now; the real blow has already fallen. No elisions.

sentences.t: Nec mortem horremus nec divom parcimus ulli.
sentences.l: Neither death do we shudder at, nor of the gods do we spare any.
sentences.i: Death does not frighten me, and there is no god I spare.
sentences.n: 'horremus', 'we shudder at', the plural 'we' for 'I'. 'divom… ulli', 'any of the gods', 'divom' the old genitive plural, with 'parcimus' taking the dative. Mezentius was called 'scorner of the gods' at his first appearance (VII.648); he will spare no god his contempt now, not even in death. Elision 'mort(em) horremus'.

sentences.t:
Desine: nam venio moriturus et haec tibi porto
dona prius.
sentences.l:
Cease: for I come to die, and these to you I bring,
gifts, first.”
sentences.i: Enough: I have come here to die, and first I bring you these gifts.”
sentences.n: The print has 'prius. ”Dixit', the closing speech mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'prius.” Dixit', corrected here: the speech ends with 'prius'. 'Desine', 'stop', leave off your threats. 'moriturus', future participle, 'about to die', 'meaning to die'. 'haec… dona', 'these gifts', said in grim irony of his javelins. 'prius', 'first', before I die. No elisions.

sentences.t: ”Dixit telumque intorsit in hostem;
sentences.l: He spoke, and a weapon he hurled at the enemy;
sentences.i: He spoke, and sent a spear spinning at his enemy;
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Mezentius's speech (see the note before). 'Dixit', 'he spoke'. 'intorsit', 'twisted, hurled', of the spin given to a thrown spear. 'in hostem', 'at the enemy'. Elision 'telumqu(e) intorsit'.

sentences.t:
inde aliud super atque aliud figitque volatque
ingenti gyro, sed sustinet aureus umbo.
sentences.l:
then another on top, and another, he plants, and he flies
in a huge circle, but holds them the golden boss.
sentences.i: then another and another after it he planted, riding round in a wide circle, but the golden boss held them all.
sentences.n: 'inde', 'then'. 'aliud super atque aliud', 'another on top and another', one after another. 'figitque volatque', 'both plants (them) and flies', the double '-que'. 'ingenti gyro', 'in a huge circle', ablative of manner; 'gyrus', a Greek word for a ring, is used of horses wheeling. 'aureus umbo', 'the golden boss', the centre of the shield Vulcan made for Aeneas (VIII.608–731); 'sustinet', 'holds up, withstands'. Elisions 'ind(e) aliud', 'atqu(e) aliud'.

sentences.t:
Ter circum adstantem laevos equitavit in orbes
tela manu iaciens, ter secum Troïus heros
immanem aerato circumfert tegmine silvam.
sentences.l:
Three times round him standing, in leftward circles he rode,
weapons with his hand hurling; three times with him the Trojan hero
a monstrous, on his bronzed covering, carries round, forest.
sentences.i: Three times he rode round him in leftward circles as Aeneas stood his ground, hurling spears; three times the Trojan hero turned, carrying round on his bronze-sheathed shield a monstrous forest of shafts.
sentences.n: 'Ter… ter', 'three times', the number repeated, as Mezentius had called three times (873). 'adstantem', 'him standing firm', Aeneas. 'laevos… in orbes', 'in leftward circles', so that his right, throwing arm faces Aeneas. 'Troïus', the diaeresis marking three syllables. 'immanem… silvam', 'a monstrous forest', the spears stuck in the shield, framing the line. 'aerato… tegmine', 'with bronzed covering', the shield. 'circumfert', 'carries round', turning on the spot to face the rider. Elisions 'circ(um) adstantem', 'imman(em) aerato'.

sentences.t:
Inde ubi tot traxisse moras, tot spicula taedet
vellere et urgetur pugna congressus iniqua,
multa movens animo iam tandem erumpit et inter
bellatoris equi cava tempora conicit hastam.
sentences.l:
Then, when of dragging out so many delays, so many spearheads, it wearies him
to pull out, and he is pressed, engaged in a fight unequal,
many things turning in his mind, now at last he bursts out, and between
the warrior horse's hollow temples he hurls his spear.
sentences.i: Then, when he grew tired of dragging out so many delays and plucking out so many spearheads, and found himself hard pressed in an uneven fight, he turned over many plans in his mind and at last broke out, and threw his spear between the hollow temples of the war-horse.
sentences.n: 'ubi… taedet', 'when it wearies (him)', the impersonal 'taedet' with the infinitives 'traxisse', 'to have dragged out', and 'vellere', 'to pull out'. 'tot… tot', 'so many… so many'. 'congressus', 'having engaged', a deponent participle. 'pugna… iniqua', 'an unequal fight', on foot against a rider circling him. 'multa movens animo', 'turning many things over in his mind'. 'erumpit', 'bursts out', from his defence. 'bellatoris equi', 'the warrior horse', the noun 'bellator' used as an adjective. In the Iliad an arrow of Paris strikes one of Nestor's horses in the head, and its plunging throws the team into confusion (Iliad 8.81–86). Elisions 'Ind(e) ubi', 'veller(e) et', 'tand(em) erumpit'.

sentences.t:
Tollit se arrectum quadrupes et calcibus auras
verberat effusumque equitem super ipse secutus
implicat eiectoque incumbit cernuus armo.
sentences.l:
Raises itself upright the four-footed beast, and with its heels the air
beats, and the thrown rider, coming down on him itself,
entangles, and with shoulder thrown out lies on him, head-first.
sentences.i: The horse reared upright and beat the air with its hooves, then, falling after its thrown rider, pinned him down, and sprawled headlong on top of him with its shoulder out of joint.
sentences.n: 'Tollit se arrectum', 'raises itself upright', rears. 'quadrupes', 'the four-footed one', a stately word for the horse. 'calcibus auras / verberat', 'beats the air with its heels', the verb held over to the next line. 'effusum… equitem', 'the rider poured out', thrown. 'super ipse secutus', 'itself following on top'. 'implicat', 'entangles'. 'eiecto… armo', ablative absolute, 'its shoulder thrown out (of joint)'. 'cernuus', 'face down, head first'. Elisions 's(e) arrectum', 'effusumqu(e) equitem', 'eiectoqu(e) incumbit'.

sentences.t: Clamore incendunt caelum Troesque Latinique.
sentences.l: With shouting they set on fire the sky, both Trojans and Latins.
sentences.i: Trojans and Latins alike set the heavens ablaze with their shouting.
sentences.n: 'Clamore incendunt caelum', 'they set the sky on fire with shouting', a bold metaphor: the noise flares up like a blaze. 'Troesque Latinique', 'both Trojans and Latins', the double '-que', Homer's 'both… and'; 'Troes' is the Greek nominative plural. Both armies see that the fight is decided. The line is hypermetric: the final '-que' of 'Latinique' is elided into 'Advolat', the first word of the next line (as at 781). Elisions 'Clamor(e) incendunt', 'Latiniqu(e) Advolat' (across the line-end).

sentences.t:
Advolat Aeneas vaginaque eripit ensem
et super haec: “Ubi nunc Mezentius acer et illa
effera vis animi?
sentences.l:
Flies up Aeneas, and from the scabbard snatches his sword,
and over him this: “Where now is Mezentius the fierce, and that
savage force of spirit?”
sentences.i: Aeneas sped to him, snatched his sword from its sheath, and standing over him said: “Where now is fierce Mezentius, and that savage force of spirit?”
sentences.n: The print has 'animi? ”Contra', the closing speech mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'animi?” Contra', corrected here: the speech ends with 'animi'. 'Advolat', 'flies to', at speed. 'vagina… eripit', 'snatches from the sheath', ablative of separation. 'super haec', 'over (him) these (words)', 'super' an adverb, with the verb of speaking left out; some take it as 'besides'. 'Ubi nunc', 'where now', a victor's taunt over a fallen enemy. 'acer', 'keen, fierce'. 'effera vis animi', 'the wild force of spirit', 'effera' from 'efferus', 'savage'. Elision 'vaginaqu(e) eripit'; 'Advolat' also takes in the elided '-que' of 895.

sentences.t:
”Contra Tyrrhenus, ut auras
suspiciens hausit caelum mentemque recepit:
sentences.l:
In reply the Tyrrhenian, when, at the air
looking up, he drank in the sky and his mind recovered:
sentences.i: The Etruscan answered, as soon as he had looked up and drunk in the air of heaven and come back to his senses:
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Aeneas's speech (see the note before). 'Contra', 'in reply', with the verb of speaking left out. 'Tyrrhenus', 'the Etruscan', Mezentius. 'ut', 'when', with the indicative. 'auras suspiciens', 'looking up at the air'. 'hausit caelum', 'drank in the sky', breathed again after his fall had stunned him. 'mentem recepit', 'recovered his mind'. No elisions.

sentences.t: “Hostis amare, quid increpitas mortemque minaris?
sentences.l: “Bitter enemy, why do you taunt me and death threaten?
sentences.i: “Bitter enemy, why do you taunt me and threaten me with death?
sentences.n: Mezentius's last speech. 'Hostis amare', vocative, 'bitter enemy'. 'increpitas', 'do you jeer', the frequentative of 'increpo', the verb used of Aeneas scolding Lausus at 810. 'mortemque minaris', 'and threaten death', 'minor' with the accusative of the thing threatened. The threat is pointless: he does not fear what is coming. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Nullum in caede nefas, nec sic ad proelia veni,
nec tecum meus haec pepigit mihi foedera Lausus.
sentences.l:
No sin in killing, nor on these terms to battle did I come,
nor with you did my Lausus strike these pacts for me.
sentences.i: Killing is no sin. I did not come to the fight on terms like these, and my Lausus struck no such bargain with you on my behalf.
sentences.n: 'Nullum in caede nefas', 'no sin in slaughter', with 'est' understood: in war, killing is no crime. 'nec sic ad proelia veni', 'nor did I come to battle on these terms', expecting mercy. 'haec… foedera', 'these treaties', a bargain to spare me. 'pepigit', perfect of 'pango', 'fixed, agreed'. 'meus… Lausus', 'my Lausus', the possessive early and the name last. 'mihi', dative of advantage, 'for me'. Elision 'Null(um) in'.

sentences.t:
Unum hoc per siqua est victis venia hostibus oro:
corpus humo patiare tegi.
sentences.l:
This one thing, by whatever there is for conquered enemies of grace, I beg:
my body with earth allow to be covered.
sentences.i: I make one plea, by whatever grace a beaten enemy may still claim: allow my body to be laid under the earth.
sentences.n: 'Unum hoc', 'this one thing', object of 'oro', 'I beg'. 'per siqua est… venia', 'by (the pardon), if there is any pardon, for conquered enemies', a compressed form of oath. 'patiare', present subjunctive, second person in '-re', 'may you allow', a polite command. 'humo tegi', 'to be covered with earth': burial, which the ancients held necessary for the soul's rest. Hector, dying, begs Achilles to give his body back for burial (Iliad 22.338–343), and is refused. Elisions 'Un(um) hoc', 'siqu(a) est', 'veni(a) hostibus'.

sentences.t:
Scio acerba meorum
circumstare odia: hunc, oro, defende furorem
et me consortem nati concede sepulchro.”
sentences.l:
I know that the bitter of my own people
surround me hatreds: this, I beg, ward off, this fury,
and me as a sharer with my son grant to the tomb.”
sentences.i: I know how bitterly my own people hate me and how close that hatred stands: protect me, I beg you, from their fury, and grant that I may lie with my son, his companion in the grave.”
sentences.n: 'Scio', 'I know', followed by the accusative and infinitive. 'acerba meorum… odia', 'the bitter hatreds of my own people', the Etruscans who drove him out. 'circumstare', 'stand round'. 'hunc… defende furorem', 'ward off this fury', 'defendo' in its old sense, 'keep off'. 'consortem nati… concede sepulchro', 'grant me to the tomb as my son's partner'; 'sepulchro' is Greenough's spelling of 'sepulcro'. Aeneas does not answer, and Virgil does not say whether the wish was granted. Elisions 'Sci(o) acerba', 'circumstar(e) odia', 'odi(a) hunc'.

sentences.t:
Haec loquitur iuguloque haud inscius accipit ensem
undantique animam diffundit in arva cruore.
sentences.l:
So he speaks, and in his throat, not unknowing, receives the sword,
and with streaming his life pours out over the fields, blood.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and, knowing what he did, took the sword into his throat; his life went streaming out over the fields with the welling blood.
sentences.n: The end of Book X. 'Haec loquitur', 'he says this'. 'iugulo', 'in his throat', ablative of place. 'haud inscius', 'not unaware', litotes: he offers his throat to the sword knowingly. 'undanti… cruore', 'with streaming gore', framing the line. 'animam diffundit', 'pours out his life', the soul imagined as carried in the blood. The Latin Library reads 'in arma', 'over his armour', for Greenough's 'in arva', 'over the fields'. Elisions 'iuguloqu(e) haud', 'undantiqu(e) animam'.
